The control costs one command. Applied within the hour to the next instrument built: before believing `intent config` had zero test coverage, the same needle was run against `doctor` and returned 3.

**AND THAT CONTROL IS NOT SUFFICIENT, WHICH I FOUND BY PASSING IT AND BEING WRONG ANYWAY** (vc, 2026-08-17). Measuring per-row parity coverage, I calibrated the needle against `wp show` before believing anything, got 3 blocks of 3 asserting output, and proceeded. **It then reported `claude hook` and `claude start` as invoked by no test in the estate. Both are false.** `claude hook` is driven inside a `run bash -c "... '$INTENT_BIN' claude hook ..."`, single-quoted; `claude start` is driven through **`$INTENT`, a different variable entirely**. The needle knew `run_intent` and `$INTENT_BIN` because those are what the calibrating case used.

**Calibration proves a needle finds what it finds. It cannot prove the needle knows every spelling, because the calibrating case is written in one of them.** A known-positive drawn from the corpus will pass any needle that handles that case's own form, and says nothing about the forms it does not share -- so the control is self-confirming in exactly the dimension that matters. **Enumerate the spellings FROM the corpus and calibrate against one of each**: `run_intent` (747), `$INTENT_BIN` bare/single/double-quoted (104), `$INTENT` (6), `bin/intent` (7). Four calibration cases, one per form, and the two false zeros became four and two real blocks.

**Note the direction, because it is the asymmetry rule again and it caught nobody by luck.** The blind needle did not lose findings -- it MANUFACTURED two, and both were the kind that read as serious (an untested hook, an untested launcher). They survived only because zeros get hand-checked here as a rule; nothing about the output distinguished them from the one real zero standing beside them.

**AND THE SHARPER FORM IS ic's, WHO HIT IT TWICE IN ONE ROUND WITH TWO SEPARATELY-WRITTEN PATTERNS** (2026-08-17, `29d6f250`). Measuring the same question in parallel, ic's needle knew `run_intent` and `bin/intent` and returned four uncovered rows; **three were false.** Going to hand-check them, ic wrote a SECOND pattern as an independent check -- **and it missed `"$INTENT"` as well**, because the closing quote sits between the variable and the path, so a pattern demanding whitespace after the variable skips it. `claude start` came back zero a second time, and was only found by grepping the literal string with no pattern at all -- **seven invocations, in a file named after the command.**

**THE CHECKER IS WRITTEN BY THE SAME HEAD AS THE NEEDLE, SO AN INDEPENDENT CHECK IS NOT INDEPENDENT UNLESS ITS SOURCE IS THE CORPUS RATHER THAN THE AUTHOR** (ic's rule, and it subsumes the one above). My version says a calibrating case is written in one spelling; ic's says the verification inherits the author's mental list of spellings whole. Together: **an instrument and its check must both draw their population FROM the corpus, because the author's memory of the corpus is the one thing they cannot help sharing.** Enumerate, then calibrate -- in that order, and never from recall.

**Two further things this episode settled, both worth more than the row count.** First, **when two instruments disagree neither is privileged** (also ic's): each is an instrument with its own subject, and the adjudication was done by hand against raw text rather than by either needle -- ic had already spent a round doubting a correct tool on the authority of a broken check whose `\bintent\s+` boundary excluded `run_intent`, ie 877 invocations. Second, **the two tools could not have found each other's finding**: ic's asks whether an invoking block asserts anything and so cannot see `agents sync`, whose eleven blocks assert plenty and discard the stdout; mine asks about output specifically and so had nothing to say about rows nobody invokes. **ic deleted theirs rather than repairing it, on Highlander grounds and not modesty -- two instruments answering one question is the violation, and a repaired second one is still a second one.**

**COUNT WHERE THE DEFECT MANIFESTS, NOT WHERE IT ORIGINATES -- AND WHEN THE SITES SHARE NO CHOKEPOINT, CREATING ONE IS THE FIX.** Issue 0050's enumeration was of the facade call sites that discard the outcome. **It went short by two**, because `ac descope` and `ac withdraw` break the call across lines and a line-oriented pattern cannot see them; cc's rule for that is that **an enumeration which has gone short cannot be checked against itself.** The constructive counterpart, measured 2026-08-17 (vc) at `ae3e308f`, after cc consolidated the arms behind one emitter: **the same property is now verifiable at ONE site.** `render.rs::reported()` is the only function in the CLI that prints a movement; the whole crate emits `ok:` from six places, four of which are not movements at all (an extract written, a store replaced, `todo.md` regenerated, an estate parsed); `intentsvcs` emits none, so the facade cannot print; and `Verdict::line` -- the one renderer that composes its own prefix -- emits `gate:`.

**The manifestation needle cannot go short in the dangerous direction, and that is the whole of the argument.** An arm that prints a movement without going through `reported()` must contain a `println!`, so it is in the swept population by construction. The origination needle has no such guarantee: an arm can call the facade in any shape a pattern fails to match, and it did, twice. **So the Highlander fix bought more than the removal of duplication -- it made the property checkable at all.** Before it, verifying "no arm reports a movement it did not make" meant enumerating twenty-one call sites correctly, with a miss invisible; after it, the same verification is "one function is the only printer", which a reader can close in a single pass.

Generalised: when a property is asserted across N sites, the cheapest true verification is at whatever chokepoint those sites share. **If they share none, that is the finding -- and building the chokepoint is a cheaper repair than building an enumeration nobody can trust.**

**A broken instrument that strengthens your finding does not get questioned; one that weakens it does.** The calibration rule above catches the first kind of error -- a zero you cannot distinguish from a dead instrument. This catches the second, and it is the more dangerous kind because nothing about it feels wrong at the time. Measured on this thread in one afternoon: a probe loop that passed one argument instead of two invented a defect in `intent wp list` that does not exist; a verb-extraction grep that omitted `sync` produced a divergence between two artefacts that in fact agree exactly; a `grep -c` for list items returned 0 against a section written as bolded paragraphs and nearly reported it empty. **All three would have made the finding stronger, and none was questioned until someone read the underlying thing instead of the count.** The asymmetry is not luck: an instrument whose error costs you a finding gets debugged; one whose error hands you a better story gets believed. Suspect your instrument hardest exactly when it agrees with what you were hoping to show.

**Success is reported by the mechanism; the property has to be checked by something else.** An edit that removes something is not verified by the edit succeeding -- two successful `Edit` calls during a board tidy silently deleted this thread's biggest finding, and it survived only because someone grepped for it afterwards. Four routes reached this shape in one day and they are one shape: a mutation that applies on a branch the test never walks; a guard scoped to what is already clean; a file clean by luck rather than by construction; and an edit whose success says nothing about what it left behind. In every case the operation returns success and the property is absent.

**A file clean by luck and a file clean by construction look identical in a diff, and only one of them stays clean.** Record what an artefact is NOT protected against, not only what it currently passes -- a green check that cannot say which kind it is has told you less than it appears to. Three routes reached this idea in one day, which is usually the sign it is load-bearing: a mutation that applies on a branch the test never walks; a guard scoped to what is already clean, which certifies the status quo; and a generated view that is formatter-stable only because nobody happened to write emphasis into it yet.

**A DEFECT WRITTEN DOWN AS THE SPECIFICATION PASSES EVERY CONSISTENCY CHECK.** Three artefacts on this estate describe behaviour that is wrong, and each one makes the wrongness harder to see rather than easier. `contract.rs`'s doc comment states _"a test-backed AC is satisfied exactly when a covering AT is GREEN"_ -- an accurate description of the `.any` it sits above and a false statement of the requirement, **so anyone checking the code against its own documentation finds agreement** (issue 0032). `cli_end_to_end.rs` asserted `status: wip` where every other surface prints `WIP`, pinning a v2 parity break as expected output until cc's sweep reached it. And the dispatch row's note for `wp show` said the output was unchanged in kind -- **which was true, and the binary was not** (cc, 2026-08-17).

**The last two are the pair worth the ink, because they sat side by side.** The estate held a correct statement of the requirement AND an incorrect assertion of it, about the same command, at the same time. **The incorrect one is the one with teeth, because it runs.** A note is read by a person at authoring time and then never again; an assertion is enforced by a machine on every commit. When the two disagree the machine wins silently and by default, because a green suite is not a report -- **nothing anywhere compares a row's prose to the assertion that covers it.** Recommended rather than ruled: where a dispatch row claims output parity, the test that covers it should quote the row, so the two statements of one requirement are forced into the same file.

**And this is why `corrected` beats `as-observed` whenever the v2 behaviour was never decided.** The register's job is to stop a v2 defect being laundered into a v3 requirement, and the laundering does not happen in the register -- it happens in a doc comment or an assertion written by someone reading the old behaviour off the old code. Both routes above produce a v3 that is internally consistent and wrong, and internal consistency is precisely what an output-equality suite measures.

**Classifying by the shape of a failure is a guess that looks like a finding** (cc, 2026-08-14, caught in their own delivered work). A red assertion tells you a test failed; it does not tell you why, and the two readings lead opposite ways -- a genuine parity break, or a test that hand-builds a v2 estate in its own body and is therefore a ratified retire under the manual-edit-workflows class. cc classified 35 rows from failure shape, then re-read the tests and found most were the second: 26 of 54 and 23 of 30 were building the old estate inline. **The register's classes are about what a test IS, not about whether it passed**, and a classification derived from a failure is the register recording the harness's state instead of the estate's. Read the test.

**`cmd | head; echo $?` reports the PAGER's exit status, never the command's** (vc, 2026-08-14, three times in one session). Exit codes are half of what this thread's parity contract is about -- D17 carries v2's codes over, INV-02 forces an override of clap's default, and the pre-commit gate reads one -- so an exit code read through a pipe is the single most load-bearing number the harness produces, and a pipeline reports the LAST stage. It manufactured two clean defects that do not exist: `intent search` with no arguments "exiting 0 on a usage error", which reads as a No Silent Errors violation and is actually exit 1; and `intent ac gate` "printing BLOCKED and exiting 0", which reads as a broken close-gate and is actually exit 1. Both were about to be reported to the node that wrote the code. Redirect to a file and read `$?` before anything else touches it, or use `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` -- and note the direction one more time: **all three artefacts handed back a finding rather than a dull result**, which is why the asymmetry rule below is the one worth re-reading before believing an instrument.

**A guard verified in one harness is not verified; it is verified in that harness** (ic, 2026-08-14, found by their own guard failing silently in the caller that mattered). The corpus guard tested green under `gen_register.sh` (`set -uo pipefail`) and was DEAD under `coverage_map.sh` (`set -euo pipefail`): the bare command substitution inside `corpus_require` aborts the shell the instant the diff reports a disagreement, so the tool exited 1 with an EMPTY stderr against a baseline known to be four files short. **A guard that dies silently in strict mode is worse than no guard -- it reads as a clean tool failure rather than as a finding.** The general shape is that shell options are part of the harness, not part of the script: `set -e` changes what a non-zero return DOES, so the same guard body has two behaviours and only one was ever exercised. Test each caller, each with its own canary, and confirm the guard names the real defect rather than merely refusing.

**Two consumers of one artefact grow two different wrong behaviours around the same missing check** (ic, 2026-08-14). `coverage_map.sh` did not merely read a stale baseline -- `[ -n "$row" ] || continue` **skipped** any file absent from it, so three files left the arithmetic entirely under a verdict that printed with full confidence, while the register's own generator went wrong a different way on the same gap. The fix is not two fixes: the comparison moved into `lib_corpus.sh` once and both callers refuse on it. **A missing check does not produce one bug; it produces one bug per consumer, and they do not look alike, so finding the first teaches you nothing about the second.**

**A count is not a diagnosis, and a record is complete only against the revision it names** (vc, 2026-08-14, caught in vc's own reported finding). A register carrying 97 rows against 98 files on disk was read as a dropped row and reported to its author as a hole in their sweep. The count was right; the cause was invented. At `309d01d` -- the revision the register names -- there were exactly 97 files, and the 98th landed at `ddac6ba`, which `git merge-base --is-ancestor` shows is not an ancestor of it. Nothing was dropped: the estate grew after the measurement, which is the record working as designed rather than failing. Two checks settle it and neither is arithmetic -- ancestry, and a set difference in **both** directions, since a phantom row and a missing one are different defects that one total conceals equally well. The generalisation is the expensive half: **any point-in-time register is falsified by the next test that lands**, and here the falsifying commit was itself a guard test written six minutes before the register was regenerated. An artefact measured at a revision must name it, and a contract consuming such an artefact must say which revision it means -- or it silently demands an estate-wide re-sweep every time anyone writes a test, which is a standard nobody can hold and everybody stops trying to.

**A file named after a command that does not test that command is worse than no file.** It answers "is this covered?" wrongly and confidently. `tests/unit/config.bats` exists, burns 5 of 7, tests configuration LOADING via `intent info` / `intent doctor` / `intent st list`, and never invokes `intent config` once -- so the command has zero coverage while the file listing implies otherwise.

**File-level classification is structurally blind to command-level coverage.** This is a stated limitation of the register, not an oversight in it: a `split` row is silent about whether any command family is exercised by nothing, because it classifies files and the question is about commands. `parity/tools/coverage_map.sh` answers that question instead, by joining the dispatch table's families against `burn-baseline.tsv` -- and the join is the method, since a naive grep reports `treeindex` as one of the best-covered families in the estate when all 53 of its tests exec the binary directly and the dispatcher sees none of them.

**A command family with zero burning coverage is a parity hole**: v3 can change it freely and the conformance suite stays green. Condition on AC-00.1; the work lives at AC-06.1.

**The burn ratio is BLIND TO NEGATIVE-ASSERTION TESTS, and the blindness is one-directional.** A test that asserts a _failure_ passes under both bindings, because `/usr/bin/false` fails too. `intent_upgrade_orchestrator.bats` runs `run "$INTENT_BIN" upgrade; assert_failure` -- it genuinely exercises the CLI and burns zero. Measured 2026-08-15: six such tests across three files, surfaced by the per-test pass as `UNCLASSIFIED / invokes CLI, zero burn` rather than found by inspection.

Two consequences worth separating. **The error direction is safe**: the method UNDER-counts CLI reach and never over-counts, so a burn figure is a floor on conformance coverage rather than an estimate of it. And **the blind spot is detectable rather than silent**: a zero-burn test that nonetheless calls the CLI is exactly the combination `classify_no_burn` refuses to classify, so these arrive as named rows wanting adjudication instead of quietly joining `out-of-scope`. A method with a known hole that reports into the hole is worth more than one whose hole is invisible.

**A fixture built to have "no git" was inside a git repository** (vc, 2026-08-15). The scratch directory this thread works in sits under `/Users/matts/.claude`, which is itself a repo, and git resolves a repository **at or above** -- correctly. So a fixture with no `.git` of its own still inherited that repo's ignore rules, and a measurement of "what happens outside git" measured something else entirely and reported it into the contract as fact. **Assert the environment you think you are in before measuring in it**: `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` costs nothing and is the difference between a fixture and a belief. Give a fixture its own `git init`, or place it where no repo is above it, and say in the record which of the two you did.

**A paired control tells you the INSTRUMENT changed, not just that the fix failed** (vc, 2026-08-15). Re-running a two-arm probe after cc's fix, both arms went silent -- including the arm that had reported before and had no reason to stop. One arm alone would have read as "the fix did not take" and been sent as such. Both arms silent is not a result about the subject at all; it is a result about the instrument, and the correct next question is what changed underneath rather than what the change proves. The discriminating pair earns its cost twice: once for the verdict, once for knowing when there is no verdict.

**Test data placed in a generated artefact is destroyed by the mechanism under test** (vc, 2026-08-15). Appending a unique phrase to `info.md` and then searching for it measured nothing: `info.md` is a generated view under D22, so `sync` regenerated it and discarded the edit -- correctly, and silently, and the subsequent empty search read exactly like a broken index. **Put test data where the truth lives**, which under D01/D02 means the canon, never a view. The general form: when the system under test owns an artefact, that artefact cannot also be your input.

**A stated cost is a claim, and it gets re-run like any other** (ic and vc, 2026-08-15, both wrong on the same number). The register sweep was described as multi-hour and not parallel-safe; that description was written into a tool's justification, quoted across nodes, and used by the verifier to REFUSE a re-sweep. Timed once, it takes **7 minutes 52 seconds**. The multi-hour figure came from a single file hanging, and a defect had been generalised into a property of the tool. Nobody had timed it. **The verifier's whole function is to re-run claims rather than read them, and a claim about cost was exempted purely because it arrived as a constraint rather than as a finding** -- constraints are the claims most worth checking, because they are the ones that stop work happening. Corollary: a deferral justified by an unmeasured cost is not a trade-off, it is a guess with a schedule attached; fix the stale row instead of noting it.

**A test written from the same misreading as the code cannot catch the misreading** (cc, 2026-08-15). A test named `both_spellings_of_sync_are_wired_and_agree` asserted the two produced identical bytes, passed, and was read as confirmation -- when all it confirmed was that a wrong model was internally consistent. `intent st sync` and `intent sync` are different commands. The incumbent's behaviour caught it, not the suite. This is the deeper form of the calibration rule: an instrument built from the hypothesis it is testing cannot falsify it, so the discriminating evidence has to come from OUTSIDE the model under test -- the v2 binary, the committed artefact, the thing that existed before the belief did.

**A check that answers confidently about a set it never looked at** (cc, 2026-08-15, naming the class the three of us hit independently in one night). Not a wrong answer -- **an answer to a different question, wearing the right answer's clothes.** Four instances, none of which announced itself: a `covers` regex written `([^-]+)` stopped dead at the hyphen in `AC-06.2`, matched zero rows, and printed a clean "nothing outstanding"; a corpus fixture keyed on `*.sql` passed identically whether or not the config under test was loaded, because the pattern was in the real global too; an ignore-needle matched `$INTENT_BIN` as a search string rather than a call site; and a green-transition check tested a file's EXISTENCE where the property wanted was that it is committed. The shared defect is that each returned a well-formed result for a population it had not established it could see. **Assert the needle matched something, and print the size of what it matched, before reporting on it** -- a count you can see is a needle you can argue with, and a zero from an unproven needle is indistinguishable from a genuinely empty result.

**Writing a rule down does not stop the author breaking it, and the evidence is this thread** (vc and cc, 2026-08-15, independently and repeatedly). vc fabricated FOUR whiteboard timestamps in one session -- while writing the clock rule, enforcing it on a peer, and citing it in the message that carried the fourth. cc read a corpus through `| head`, lost the eleventh of eleven rows, and published "ten spellings" into a source comment and a commit message -- with `| head` already on their own board as a watch-out, three lines from the pipeline-exit-code note, added in that same session. Neither failure was ignorance of the rule; in both cases the author had written it that day.

**So a rule that depends on the author remembering it at the moment of use is not a control, it is a hope with good phrasing.** The two remedies that actually worked here were both mechanical and neither required anyone to remember anything: the pre-commit clock guard REFUSED a bad stamp, and `lib_corpus.sh` REFUSED a register generated against an incomplete baseline. The two that failed were both documentation. This is the general form of D30's timestamp argument and of the guard-rather-than-a-promise choice made throughout this thread -- **when a rule matters, spend the effort on the mechanism that enforces it rather than on the sentence that states it**, and treat a rule you can only obey by concentrating as an unfixed defect rather than a solved problem.

**A generated artefact that cannot be re-derived from committed state has no cheap check, and its stamp is the only guard it has** (vc, proposed 2026-08-15; ic, evidenced the same day). Not a theoretical class. The 26 `cmd-*.md` command inventories are generated by `gen_inventory.sh` from `probes/toplevel.tsv` -- a file the script only ever READS, which lives in a throwaway scratch directory, has **never been tracked**, and is no longer on disk anywhere. So the input behind the committed measurement at `69d42a7` is gone, and those 26 artefacts can be checked for provenance (do they all name one revision?) and not for content. **That is a materially weaker claim than the drift check has been assumed to rest on**, because the inventory is the measurement half of the comparison the table is checked against: the authored side is fully checked and the side it is compared to is not.

**CORRECTION, 2026-08-15 (ic): "gone" was wrong -- it was UNTRACKED, which is a different thing, and looking is cheaper than reasoning about it.** The paragraph above concluded the input no longer existed anywhere on disk. It was still sitting in the originating session's scratch directory, along with the ad-hoc driver that produced it, the fake HOME it ran under, and the sandbox. `git log --all` was the right query for "was this ever committed" and the wrong one for "does this exist"; nothing had been run against the filesystem. **The TSV is now recovered and COMMITTED at `parity/probes/toplevel.tsv`**, which is what the rule asked for all along, and the driver is committed beside it as `tools/probe_toplevel.sh` -- it had never existed as a file.

**With the real input back, the 26 inventories were checked for content and are exactly faithful to it: 26 of 26 reproduce, modulo table padding.** So the weaker claim was true of the record and not of the artefacts. Three further findings from the same run, all measured:

- **Exit codes reproduce 26 of 26 at the same revision; first lines 26 of 26 in behaviour.** Byte counts reproduce 20 of 26 -- the six that move (`bootstrap`, `doctor`, `ext`, `help`, `info`, `todo`) embed the sandbox's ABSOLUTE PATH in their output, and `ext` differs by exactly the path-length delta, 55 bytes against 55 characters. **The byte column is a property of the path the probe ran under, and that path was never recorded.** Exit codes and first lines are the portable half.
- **`probe.sh` isolated `INTENT_HOME` and not `HOME`, and got away with it because the uncommitted driver did `export HOME="$SP/fakehome"` before sourcing it.** When that driver went, the isolation went with it: a re-probe written against the committed file alone read the developer's real `~/.intent/ext` and took a different code path. This is this document's own mechanism-over-sentence rule turned on itself -- **the isolation that was written down survived and the one that lived in someone's shell history did not.** Now in `probe.sh` where a caller cannot forget it.
- **The probe matrix MUTATES ITS OWN SANDBOX and is therefore not idempotent.** `intent todo` bare generates `intent/todo.md` when absent, so run one records `no intent/todo.md yet -- generating...` and run two records the read path -- two runs of one script at one revision disagreeing on a first line, with nothing in the output saying which run it was. The driver now rebuilds the sandbox rather than reusing it. Same command, same reason its dispatch-table row is classified `mutate`.
- **The provenance's "108-probe matrix" is right and the inventory renders 104 of them.** The 27th unit is `version`: probed on 2026-08-14, never given a `cmd-version.md`, because `gen_inventory.sh`'s spec list has no entry for it. Measured data exists for a command the inventory does not carry.

**Worse, the artefact instructs the reader to destroy it.** Every generated header says _"re-run it rather than editing this file"_ -- correct advice that, once the input vanished, would have overwritten 26 good measurements with empty probe fields carrying the revision stamp of the good data. Measured rather than assumed: `awk` against a missing file exits 2 and produces **nothing**, so the dash fallback never runs, and the script's `set -uo pipefail` without `-e` does not stop it. The remedy is the one this section keeps arriving at -- `gen_inventory.sh` now REFUSES on a missing or empty TSV, because **a missing measurement must present as a refusal to measure, never as a measurement of nothing.** The general rule for anyone adding a generator here: if the input is not committed, the output is stamp-only, and saying so in the record is part of producing it.

**RE-DERIVABILITY IS NOT COMPLETENESS, and a lossy generator is a perfect fixed point with itself** (ic, 2026-08-15). The skew check asks whether a committed view matches what its generator PRODUCES. A generator that silently drops a field satisfies that for ever: regenerate, compare, identical, green. Measured on `dispatch-table.md` -- the canon carried **20 distinct `target` sub-fields and the renderer named 5**, so 15 were written, committed and invisible in the human-readable face, including config keys another node was blocked on. **The check was not wrong; it was answering a different question faithfully**, which is the hardest kind to notice because nothing ever contradicts it. Two properties, two checks: skew for re-derivability, and a completeness refusal comparing the canon's own keys against the rendered text. The corollary for this toolchain: **every generator wants to be asked "does the view carry everything the canon holds?", separately from "does the view match the generator?"** -- and the second cannot answer the first.

**ENUMERATE THE POPULATION; DO NOT SNIFF FOR A MARKER** (ic, 2026-08-15). A needle reports on the set it MATCHED, never the set it was aimed at -- so before building a check on one, count what it matches and print the count. Measured: a backstop planned around detecting a `GENERATED` banner would have covered **1 file in 30**, because 29 generated views carry no banner; enumerating the apparatus directories instead covered all 30. The same shape twice more the same day -- a `jq '.families[].entries[]'` audit reported a canon clean while every offending string sat in a top-level array that path does not traverse, and a mutation run went red from a **different guard entirely** because the fixture never reached the branch under test. **A structured query is a needle too**, and it reports on the subtree it walked. The discipline is cheap and mechanical: derive the population from something that must be complete (a directory listing, the canon's own keys, a declared roster), never from a property the members happen to carry, and **assert the fixture reached the branch before reading its verdict**.

**A GUARD POSITIONED AFTER THE WRITE CAN ONLY CATCH THE SUBSET OF FABRICATIONS THAT ARE ALSO IMPLAUSIBLE** (cc, 2026-08-17, from their own fabricated stamp; attributed by MECHANISM rather than by node, at cc's request, because the clock is one instance of it and not the point). cc wrote a heartbeat of `15:03Z` as an estimate rather than a clock read. **The clock guard would have been GREEN on it**: check A refuses a stamp in the FUTURE, and an estimate that lands in the PAST is exactly the failure the protocol names first and the one no clock comparison can see. What rescued it was ordering -- check C, which compares two board stamps to each other and needs no clock at all.

Generalise off the clock and it is a positional claim about controls: **a guard that runs after the value exists is testing the value, and a fabricated value that happens to be plausible is indistinguishable from a real one by any test of the value alone.** Three instances, deliberately from three different layers:

- **the clock guard** -- refuses a future stamp; blind to a plausible past one, which is why check C (stamp-against-stamp, no clock) is the one that closes it;
- **the corpus loader that refuses before the path is written** rather than validating the file after -- the fixture cannot be produced wrong, so there is no wrong fixture to detect;
- **cc's guards-unmet driver refusing a self-loop-capable edge before driving it** (2026-08-17) -- the table will not accept a guarded edge whose `from` contains its own target, instead of driving it and interpreting the result.

**The remedy is not a better guard, it is an earlier one**: move the control to the point where the wrong value cannot be produced, and the class of things you must detect afterwards is empty rather than merely smaller. Where that is impossible, prefer a control that compares two artefacts to EACH OTHER over one that compares an artefact to a standard -- the same move as an equality between opposed enumerators, one axis over.

**EVERY ARTEFACT RECORDS THE NAME IT WAS BUILT TO CARRY AND NEVER A REFERENT FOR WHAT IT WAS BUILT FROM** (dc, 2026-08-17, generalising issue 0049 off verdicts and onto artefacts). 0049 was a runner reporting a leg verdict without recording whether the tree moved under it. dc found the same defect twice more in one afternoon, in artefacts rather than in reports:

- **a signed binary that cannot name its commit.** `int macos stage` records `commit: <HEAD>` and `traceable: yes`, where traceable means the working tree is clean -- and it never asks when the binaries were BUILT, because `stage` copies them rather than building them. Measured live and unplanted: HEAD at `2026-08-17T15:11:14Z`, `intent` built three hours earlier, `intentd` built **forty-two hours** earlier. Commit the tree and the whole chain goes green over bytes from two different earlier trees.
- **a vendored tree that cannot name its source.** `int vendor` compares the vendored files against a manifest that ships beside them and **is rewritten by the same act that changes them** -- so a re-vendor and a local patch produce the identical `27 of 27`. **This is the sibling class in its purest form**: the detection question answers itself, because the other state producing this output is a locally-patched tree whose manifest was regenerated. The manifest's own provenance field cannot separate them either: `devbin_version: 0.1.0` does not move with commits, so **the field that exists to carry provenance is constant across exactly the thing it is meant to distinguish.**

**The corollary is a rule about where a provenance claim may be read from: an artefact must assert its own provenance, and the assertion must be read FROM THE ARTEFACT, never from a record written beside it.** A manifest states what was MEANT to be built; only the artefact can answer what was. dc's own `staged_version` already argues this one function over -- read the version from the BINARY, never from a manifest -- so the rule generalises a discipline the layer already keeps in one place and not the others.

**And the ruling that goes with it, because the tempting fix is the wrong one** (vc, 2026-08-17, on dc's ask): this does NOT strengthen the checksum criterion it was found under. That row's criterion is _the published hash matching the published bytes_, and stale binaries satisfy it perfectly -- the hash is honest, the commit attribution is not. Folding a provenance control under a checksum row makes a green start meaning something the row's text does not say, **which is the third axis arriving inside a remedy.** dc declined to do it unprompted; the finding gets its own row instead.

**AND THE TENSE AXIS: A GREEN PRODUCED BY UNCOMMITTED STATE IS A GREEN NOBODY ELSE CAN REPRODUCE** (dc, 2026-08-17, correcting their own report of the vendor instance above, and vc's explanation of it). Asked of the vendored tree, _what other state would produce this same output?_ has a second answer neither of us gave: **an uncommitted regeneration.** A tree that agrees with itself because someone re-derived the record locally is indistinguishable from a tree that agrees because it is correct.

Measured, not constructed. At HEAD `702b58f8` the committed `bin/devbin` is `41017e54` and the manifest committed beside it records `8016f112`, so **a fresh clone reports DIVERGED right now** -- while every local check ran green, because a manifest regeneration sitting uncommitted in the worktree had made the local tree self-consistent. `upstream/main` at `5765c5da` is clean, so nothing broken is published, **and that is hv's CI-budget freeze rather than any control -- recorded as luck, because filing it as a save teaches the opposite of what happened.**

**Two axes, one root.** `devbin_version: 0.1.0` being constant across the thing it distinguishes is the FIELD-level failure; the worktree agreeing while the commit does not is the TENSE-level failure. The corollary is the same one the clock guard reached from the other end: **verify against what the COMMIT holds, for the same reason check C blocks only on the stamps the commit adds.**

**And the instance is the class catching its own reporter, through the instrument built for it.** dc filed the `stage` defect -- a control that records a clean tree and never asks when the bytes were built -- and reported `27 of 27, stock devbin` in the same afternoon. That report was true of the worktree and false of the commit: the identical tense error, one lane over, about their own lane. **A rule you have just written down is not yet a rule you apply.**

### THE PARITY MEASUREMENT HAS EXACTLY ONE REAL EXECUTION, AND IT IS MINUTES WIDE (vc, 2026-08-18, measured not reasoned)

**The v2-versus-v3 comparison that this whole contract is built on becomes UNRUNNABLE the moment the hoist lands, and nothing in the plan carried that constraint until it was driven.** The migration writes `"intent_version": "3.0.0-dev"` into `intent/.config/config.json`; `bin/intent` grew a forward-compatibility guard at `53f88757` that refuses a project from the future. Run v2's gate against an already-migrated tree and it exits 2:

```
error: this project declares Intent v3.0.0-dev, and this is Intent v2.19.0
  'ac' would write to a project built by a newer Intent than this one understands
```

**The guard is correct and must not change.** The consequence is procedural: **after cutover there is no v2 half, so v2-versus-v3 parity can never be measured again on this project.** Every rehearsal to date -- including the byte-identical run at `6248236e` -- is a rehearsal of a measurement that gets one execution, immediately before the hoist, on the actual tree being hoisted.

**How it was found is the argument rather than a footnote: the guard is in `bin/intent_helpers`, the gate is three files away, and the link between them is a config value written by a third program.** No amount of reading connects those three. One command did. This is the same lever that produced every real finding of 2026-08-18 across all four nodes.

**THE PROCEDURE, and every control in it exists because its absence produced a wrong green at least once:**

1. **Clone the repo at the exact commit being hoisted and assert `dirty=0` BEFORE building.** A clean tree asserted after the build tells you nothing about what the build compiled.
2. **Build v3 INSIDE that clone, with its own target directory.** A binary from a shared `target/` cannot be shown to have come from the commit under test -- and a fixture once passed only because cargo had put the binary inside the repository.
3. **Run v2's gate over the FILES first, before migrating.** This is the half that ceases to exist afterwards; taking it second is taking it never.
4. **Migrate, capturing stdout as the dispositions record.** Without `--dispositions` a conservation run counts every declared drop as loss -- measured at `ALTERED 112`, all of them ratified template removals.
5. **Run v3's gate over the STORE.**
6. **Delete every `.md` under `intent/st` and score again, printing the surviving `.md` count IN THE SAME BREATH as the score.** Asserting the deletion at deletion time is not the control: a store falling back to files still on disk returns the right number for the wrong reason. Note that the migration itself WRITES markdown, so this step deletes the generated views as well as the sources.
7. **Compare with `diff`, not by eye and not by count.** The three outputs are expected byte-identical -- traversal artefacts included, such as `AC-08.8` printing before `AC-08.7`. **Set equality is the weak test; the ordering fingerprint is the strong one, because a reimplementation that merely agreed would not reproduce v2's traversal.**

**BOTH HALVES RUN ON ONE TREE OR IT IS NOT A COMPARISON.** Measured on separate trees, a disagreement is ambiguous between "v3 regressed" and "the contract moved", and no amount of care separates them afterwards. The `46/114` figure quoted for three days was pinned at `bcbd02cd` while five of five components -- `legacy.rs`, `contract.rs`, `store.rs`, `model.rs`, `facade.rs` -- and `acceptance.md` itself had all moved under it.

**TIMING IS NOT PART OF THIS MEASUREMENT.** Machine load moves it by more than an order of magnitude and it proves nothing about parity. Record it if convenient; never publish a speedup from a run whose load was not controlled.

# Parity inventory (ST0056 / WP-01, AC-01.3) -- the IC deep pass

> Measured against `69d42a7` on 2026-08-14 by ic. Every figure here names the revision it was taken at, and every file in this directory is regenerated by `tools/gen_inventory.sh` rather than edited. A measured number that cannot be re-run is a rumour with a decimal point -- the "314 AT rows" figure sat in three documents and was wrong by 5x.

## What this is

The flag-level half of the parity contract: for every command in `../parity.md`'s command-level table, the subcommand set, the flag grammar, and the observed stdout / stderr / exit-code behaviour. One file per command.

## Method

Four sources, in descending authority, with every disagreement recorded as a finding rather than resolved by picking a winner:

| #   | Source                                                                                                 | What it is good for         | Why it is not trusted alone                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | Runtime probes (108 invocations, four per command: bare, `--help`, an unknown flag, outside a project) | What the tool actually does | Cannot see unreachable code                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| 2   | Main dispatch `case` arms                                                                              | What the source intends     | Arm indentation is inconsistent across `bin/` -- `intent_todo:384` sits at column 0 while `intent_st:295` nests, so one indentation-anchored regex scored the 1621-line `intent_st` at **zero** subcommands |
| 3   | Arg-parsing `case` arms at any depth                                                                   | The flag grammar            | Says nothing about which verb a flag belongs to                                                                                                                                                             |
| 4   | `lib/help/*.help.md`                                                                                   | Documentation               | Covers 11 of 27 scripts; its `@usage`/`@options`/`@arguments` grammar is used by exactly **one** file; it still describes `upgrade` as "Upgrade from STP to Intent v2.1.0" at v2.19.0                       |

Probes ran against a detached worktree with `INTENT_HOME` passed explicitly. `bin/intent:12` only self-resolves `INTENT_HOME` when it is unset, so an inherited value silently points the whole run at the developer's live tree -- the first probe run did exactly that before the harness was corrected.

## Corrections to `../parity.md`'s command-level table

vc's table flagged the `at` set and the aliases as unverified. All are now verified by invocation.

| Row            | Table said                                                           | Measured                                                                                                                                                                          | Evidence                                                                           |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `at`           | `lint [--fix], set, list`                                            | **`list, lint, red, green, na, done, notdone`** -- there is **no `set` verb**; `cmd_at_set` is an internal function, and `done`/`notdone` are aliases for `green`/`red`           | `intent_acceptance:1343-1349`; `intent at set` -> `error: unknown at command: set` |
| `st`           | `new, start, done, cancel, list, sync, organize, show, edit, repair` | adds **`zero`** (`intent st zero` -> `Usage: intent st zero install`, exit 0)                                                                                                     | `intent_st` dispatch; verified by invocation                                       |
| `lang`         | `init, remove, list`                                                 | adds **`show`**, **`sync`**, and **`rm`** (alias of `remove`)                                                                                                                     | `intent lang sync` -> `ok: no declared languages; nothing to sync`                 |
| `claude rules` | `list/show [--lang]`                                                 | adds **`validate`** and **`index`**                                                                                                                                               | `intent claude rules index` -> `ok: indexed 64 rules`                              |
| `issues`       | `list, add (alias new), show, close, open`                           | confirmed, plus an undocumented **`help`** verb                                                                                                                                   | `intent issues new` -> `error: Issue title is required`, identical to `add`        |
| `organise`     | listed as an alias to verify                                         | **Not a top-level alias.** `intent organise` -> `error: Unknown command 'organise'`. The alias exists only one level down, at `intent st organise`, normalised at `intent_st:290` | measured both                                                                      |

## Cross-cutting findings

**1. `intent organize` and `intent st organize` are two different implementations, and MODULES.md registers both.** Row 15 gives `bin/intent_st` an `organize` verb; row 31 gives `bin/intent_organize` the same job. Against one steel thread in a fresh project they print different things and share no output: the top-level form reports `ok: moved 0, kept 0` plus per-directory counts (117B), the `st` form reports `Already organized: ST0001 in intent/st/NOT-STARTED` (73B). A Highlander violation recorded in the registry that exists to prevent it. **v3 must implement one of them; which one is an hv decision, not a port-time coin toss.**

**2. About a fifth of v2's failure paths write to the wrong stream.** Across 108 probes, failing invocations split **45 stderr-only, 12 stdout-only, 2 both**. This is the same class as the already-queued ruling on the three plugin bins writing `Error:` to stdout, and it is larger than that ruling's three known sites. An error on stdout interleaves with captured command output, which is how a voice becomes data.

**3. `--help` reports failure on 10 of 27 commands.** Two shapes: usage printed to **stdout with exit 1** (`init`, `st`, `wp`, `todo`, `treeindex`, `fileindex`), and an error to stderr (`ac`, `at`, `help`, `claude`). `intent at --help` is parsed as an unknown verb. `intent help --help` fails outright. Asking for help and being told you failed is a defect in v2 and a decision for v3: reproduce faithfully, or deviate.

**4. Three commands accept an unknown flag silently with exit 0.** `intent info --zzz-not-a-flag`, `intent config --zzz-not-a-flag` (zero output) and `intent version --zzz-not-a-flag` all succeed. **This one cannot be reproduced by accident**: clap rejects unrecognised arguments by default and exits 2, so v3 will diverge here on day one whether or not anyone decides to. It needs a ratified deviation before WP-05, not a triage note during it.

**5. The project-context gate is uniform; the plugin bypass is not.** Fourteen commands refuse outside a project with exactly `error: not in an Intent project directory` (`bin/intent:206`). Two do not: `claude` never reaches the gate because plugin commands exec before the project check (`bin/intent:188-191`), and `upgrade` supplies its own message. `agents` runs outside a project for the same plugin-bypass reason despite not being in `GLOBAL_COMMANDS`.

**6. Observed exit codes are 0, 1 and 2 only**, and the only 2 observed in the shipped surface came from `intent critic` (`intent_critic:89,95`). `bin/release` also uses 2 but is out of parity scope. `intent claude hook` propagates a hook's own exit code, including 2, by design.

**7. `intent claude rules index` writes into `INTENT_HOME`, not the project.** It modified a tracked file (`intent/plugins/claude/rules/index.json`) in the worktree under test. A command that reads as a query mutates the installation.

**8. Seventeen of 26 commands have no help file at all.** `ac`, `at`, `bootstrap`, `config`, `critic`, `doctor`, `help`, `info`, `init`, `issues`, `llm`, `organize`, `st`, `st_zero`, `todo`, `treeindex`, `upgrade`. Naming drift too: `stzero.help.md` against `bin/intent_st_zero`, and `rules.help.md` documents a `claude` subcommand rather than a top-level one. WP-05 generates help from the dispatch table, which retires this whole class -- but it means **`lib/help/` cannot be used as the v2 spec to port from**.

**9. The per-command files are named `cmd-<command>.md`, not `<command>.md`.** Two command names collide with filenames the toolchain treats as special, and macOS matches case-insensitively: a generated `claude.md` is loaded as this directory's `CLAUDE.md` and injected into every subsequent session as instructions (observed, not theorised -- it happened here), and `agents.md` shadows the `AGENTS.md` convention the same way. The prefix makes the collision unconstructible instead of special-casing two known names. **Worth carrying into v3**: any generated-view filename derived from user or command data can land on a reserved name, and the v3 view renderer will generate far more files than this.

## Contract gaps for vc

Per the work order, these fit no ratified deviation class and are flagged rather than judged here:

1. **The two `organize` implementations** (finding 1). Not a deviation class -- a v2 defect the port must resolve. Needs an hv ruling on which survives.
2. **Silent acceptance of unknown flags** (finding 4). Guaranteed divergence under clap. Needs its own ratified class; "file layout" and the other three classes do not cover a _voice and exit-code_ change.
3. **`--help` exiting non-zero** (finding 3). Same shape: a deliberate, ratified deviation is the honest option, but the register has no class for "v2 behaviour we are fixing rather than porting".

Gaps 2 and 3 point at the same hole: the four ratified classes in `parity.md` all describe **layout and workflow** changes. There is no class for **a v2 behaviour that is simply wrong and will be corrected**, which is what the stream, exit-code and unknown-flag findings all need. Proposed name: **`corrected`** -- distinct from `deviate` in that `deviate` is a design consequence and `corrected` is a bug fix, and both must carry a ratification reference.

## Re-running

```
SP=<scratch> WT=<worktree> OUTDIR=intent/st/ST0056/parity bash tools/gen_inventory.sh
```

`tools/probe.sh` captures the runtime matrix; `tools/extract_verbs.sh` and `tools/extract_flags.sh` do the static passes. All three refuse to run against a missing worktree or sandbox rather than emitting a uniform empty surface that reads like data.

# v2-authored AT rows -- the corpus v3 did not produce

**Supplied by vc, 2026-08-17, for issue 0056's permanent regression test. Captured, not written.**

## Why this exists at all

Issue 0056's closing section states the requirement and the reason:

> A regression test must assert **byte-equality against a fixture written in v2's spelling** -- not that ingest-then-emit is stable, which it already is.

**`n-a` re-ingests to `Na` and re-emits to `n-a`, so from pass 2 the round trip is a fixed point.** A stability test seeded from v3's own output reports a clean pass and is RIGHT. The general form, which outlives this issue: _a stability property measured from the system's own output confirms that the system is consistent with itself, which is exactly what a one-time normalisation preserves._

**So the seed must be a corpus v3 did not produce.** Two weaker candidates were rejected on the way here, and the reasons matter more than the choice:

- **`display()` itself.** `view_determinism.rs`'s first regression test asserted `view.contains(format!("status: {}", status.display()))` -- comparing the renderer to the function that _defines_ the renderer's spelling. `display()` returning `n@a` passed it. True, and unable to discriminate.
- **A hand-authored seed.** vc generated one for the manual pairing on 2026-08-17: a real v2.19.0 project, real v2 templates, linting clean at 4/4. **Rejected as a committed fixture by its own author**, because it was written _for this test_ -- one degree closer to the thing under test than a fixture may be. Its authority would be vc's judgement about v2's grammar rather than v2's own output.

**The rows below have an authority neither node supplied: they were authored under v2, they have lived in this repository's committed canon, and every one of them predates issue 0056.**

## Provenance

| source                                       | commit     | authored   | statuses   | rows |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---- |
| `intent/st/COMPLETED/ST0054/acceptance.md`   | `f28938c2` | 2026-08-13 | `n/a`      | 3    |
| `intent/st/NOT-STARTED/ST0046/acceptance.md` | `f28938c2` | 2026-08-13 | `to-write` | 9    |
| `intent/st/COMPLETED/ST0045/acceptance.md`   | `ee44f63b` | 2026-08-14 | `green`    | 2    |

Issue 0056 was filed **2026-08-17**. `AtStatus::display()` landed at **`d14cd0b5`**, the same day. **Every row here was last written before either event**, so no row can have been shaped by the defect or by its fix.

## `red` IS ABSENT AND THAT IS A DECLARED GAP, NOT AN OVERSIGHT

Measured across the estate at `3ce298c3`, constrained to column-0 `- AT-` rows: **140 `green`, 62 `to-write`, 22 `n/a`, 4 `red`.**

**All four `red` rows live in `intent/st/ST0056/acceptance.md`**, the thread being edited today -- so there is no uncontaminated source for that variant and this fixture does not fabricate one.

**A test standing on this corpus must SAY so rather than read as four-of-four.** `red` is one of the three variants where the wire tag and the authored form COINCIDE, and **that coincidence is the entire hiding mechanism of issue 0056** -- echoing the wrong source is correct for `green` and `red` and wrong only for `n/a`. So a reader must not infer from a green that all four were compared against authored bytes. **Three compared against the corpus; one against a transcription; stated as such.**

## The discriminating row, named so it is not optimised away

**`ST0046` AT-01.1's note contains the row separator.**

```
-- status: to-write -- red-first; modules check -- unregistered fixture flagged
```

The note is introduced by a spaced `--` and then **contains another spaced `--`**. v2's grammar handles this by never parsing the note (`AT_G_NOTE='( -- .*)?'` is greedy to end-of-line). **Any v3 reader that splits on `--` rather than anchoring the status will round-trip this row wrongly**, and it will do so silently, because the two halves still look like a note. **Nine of nine ST0046 rows carry the same shape** -- corrected from "eight of the nine" by cc, 2026-08-17, and re-measured here: every `to-write` row is `status: to-write -- red-first; modules <check|sync> -- <text>`. It changes nothing about the hazard and it is recorded because a count in a fixture README is a claim someone will scope a test to.

This is the row most likely to fail and therefore the row worth keeping. **Do not "simplify" the fixture by dropping it.**

## What a test built on this should assert

**Parse each line through the v2 reader, render it through `views`, and require the output byte to equal the input byte.** Not `contains`, not a status-token comparison: the whole line. A status check would pass on a row whose coverage list or note had been reordered, and the covers list and the note are the two fields issue 0033 already destroys elsewhere.

The rows live in `rows.txt`, one per line, verbatim, no trailing edits. Regenerate by re-capturing from the commits above -- never by rendering them.

# Per-test register for the pending files (ST0056 / WP-05, AC-05.3)

> Measured at `c60cdbd` by ic. Generated by `tools/gen_pertest.sh` from the TAP `tools/burn.sh` captured under `BURN_TAP_DIR`; do not hand-edit rows.

## What a row means

A **pending** file mixes tests that reach the CLI with tests that do not. The file-level register says so honestly and cannot say more; this table names which is which, so WP-05 can point the reaching half at the v3 binary and treat the rest on its merits.

The split is **measured, not read**. Under the default binding every test passes; under `INTENT_BIN=/usr/bin/false` exactly the tests that reach the CLI fail. So the mutant run's `not ok` set is the burning set, by name, with no assertion-parsing involved.

| the mutant run says | meaning                                 | class                                     |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `not ok`            | the test's result depends on the binary | **keep** -- real conformance coverage     |
| `ok`                | the binary is irrelevant to it          | classified by why, using the shared rules |

**One class of row is NOT measured, and says so.** A test asserting a FAILURE passes under both bindings, because `/usr/bin/false` fails too -- so the burn ratio is structurally blind to it and a zero there means "the instrument cannot see this", not "this does not reach the CLI". Those rows carry **`basis: read, not measured`**, are **excluded from every burn arithmetic**, and are **counted separately** in the tally (vc ruling, 2026-08-15). The register's authority is that it never reads assertions; that holds for every measured row, and these sit visibly outside it rather than quietly inside. The blindness is one-directional -- burn under-counts CLI reach and never over-counts -- so every burn figure here is a FLOOR.

Files whose class was **decided by ruling** rather than measured are listed at the foot and deliberately not split: per-test rows would quietly contradict the ruling the file row carries.

# Keep / retire / deviate register -- first pass (ST0056 / WP-01, AC-01.3)

> Measured at `c60cdbd` by ic. Regenerated by `tools/gen_register.sh` from `tools/burn.sh` output; do not hand-edit rows.

## How each row was decided

The classification axis is the **burn ratio**: each file is run twice, once with the default `INTENT_BIN` and once with `INTENT_BIN=/usr/bin/false`, and the delta is the number of tests that actually reach the top-level CLI.

This is empirical where reading assertions is inferential, and the difference is not academic. `treeindex_commands.bats` reads as 53 CLI tests and is in fact 53 tests that exec `bin/intent_treeindex` directly, bypassing the dispatcher entirely; its burn is zero. `claude_with_intent.bats` read as a CLI test, reported zero burn, and turned out to alias the binary through an unbraced `$INTENT_BIN_DIR/intent` that the retarget sweep had missed -- **the burn measurement found a hole in the retarget that four separate grep passes did not.**

| burn                                  | meaning                                     | class                                                       |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| all tests                             | the file exercises the CLI and nothing else | **keep** -- runs unmodified against `INTENT_BIN`            |
| zero, and it calls `bin/intent_<sub>` | tests an entry point v3 will not have       | **deviate** -- semantic rewrite, not a path swap            |
| zero, and it sources a shell file     | unit-tests a bash function                  | **retire** -- dies with the shell                           |
| zero, and it never invokes the CLI    | pins this repo's own content                | **out-of-scope** -- not a conformance test                  |
| some                                  | mixed concerns in one file                  | **pending** -- needs per-test rows before WP-05 leans on it |
| any, but baseline not green           | the delta carries no information            | **UNCLASSIFIED**                                            |

A file matching no rule is emitted UNCLASSIFIED rather than assigned a best guess. A wrong `retire` is coverage that disappears at the cut with nobody watching, which is the defect the AT grammar existed to kill; the refuse-lossy discipline applies to classification exactly as it applies to migration.

**Vocabulary (vc ruling, 2026-08-14): `keep · retire · deviate · pending`, shared verbatim with the dispatch table at `surface/dispatch-table.json`, with `pending` written explicitly and never implied by omitting a field.** Absence-as-meaning is un-greppable and reads as an oversight. The payoff is that **AC-05.3 becomes mechanical rather than eyeballed**: no row carries `pending` at close.

This pass renames `split` to `pending`. Nothing is lost -- the reason a row is pending was always carried by the `basis` column (`partial burn`), not by the class name, so the name was free to become the one the other artefact uses.

**Two values sit outside that four, deliberately, and ic flagged the divergence rather than collapsing it.** `out-of-scope` and `UNCLASSIFIED` are not dispositions on the same axis as the other four:

- `out-of-scope` answers _is this in the parity contract at all_ -- a decided answer, not a deferred one. Folding it into `keep` would claim a repo-content test is part of the conformance suite; folding it into `retire` would schedule a perfectly good test for deletion. Neither is true, and the orthogonal axis is real.
- `UNCLASSIFIED` is a MEASUREMENT FAILURE, not a deferred decision: the baseline was not green, so the burn delta means nothing. It must be zero at close for the same reason `pending` must, but the remedy is different -- `pending` needs a judgement, `UNCLASSIFIED` needs a working measurement.

**Scope note:** `pending` is a first-pass verdict, not a final one. Those files carry both portable and non-portable tests and need per-test rows; this pass deliberately stops at the file level rather than guessing which half is which.

## The `v3 exposure` column -- a SECOND predicate, orthogonal to burn

Burn asks whether a file reaches the **v2** CLI. Both of its runs are v2, one with the binary redirected, so it structurally cannot ask whether the file's own SETUP survives v3's file layout. Those are different questions and only the first was being measured -- which means `keep` was quietly promising something its evidence never established. A file can burn 12/12, earn `keep`, and fail every one of those tests under v3 **before a single assertion runs**, because its fixture wrote to a directory v3 does not have.

Found by cc from the v3 side (2026-08-14): they ran the `keep` set against the real v3 binary and got files where 17 of 17 reds trace to one cause in `setup`. This column is the v2-side half, computed statically by `tools/fixture_probe.sh` so both predicates sit on one row.

| value        | what it means                                               | remedy                                                                                                                       |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `none`       | no literal v2 estate path                                   | nothing -- burn's verdict stands                                                                                             |
| `status-dir` | writes `intent/st/{COMPLETED,NOT-STARTED,CANCELLED}/`       | v3 holds status as a FIELD in `st/<ID>/thread.json`; there is no such directory, so the write fails outright                 |
| `gen-view`   | hand-writes an `info.md` / `acceptance.md` under an st path | v3 GENERATES both. Worse than a failed write: it succeeds and is then outvoted by regeneration, or refused by the skew check |

**The two are not the same repair, and merging them overstates the cost.** A file that hand-builds the estate with `mkdir` converts to CLI-built fixtures, which is real work. A file that builds through the CLI and then reaches in at a literal path needs the path resolved, which is not. Several of the exposed files are the second kind and read as the first.

**This column reports EXPOSURE, not breakage.** Whether a given file actually goes red under v3 is a v3-side question owned by whoever runs it there; what is measurable from here is whether the file hardcodes a layout assumption at all -- the necessary condition, not the sufficient one. Reading it as the latter would repeat, in a new column, exactly the error it exists to correct.

Authored prose (`design.md`, `impl.md`, `tasks.md`) stays authored in v3, so fixtures touching those are deliberately not flagged.

#!/bin/bash
# burn.sh -- classify the BATS estate by BURN RATIO.
#
# Method: run each file twice, once with the default INTENT_BIN and once with
# INTENT_BIN=/usr/bin/false, and count failures each time. The delta is the
# number of tests that actually reach the top-level CLI.
#
#   burn == total     the whole file exercises the CLI          -> keep candidate
#   burn == 0         the file never reaches the CLI at all     -> retire/out-of-scope
#   0 < burn < total  mixed; needs per-test adjudication        -> split candidate
#
# This is empirical where assertion-parsing is inferential. A file can call
# run_intent and still assert only on repo content; a file can look CLI-shaped
# and actually exec bin/intent_treeindex, bypassing the dispatcher entirely
# (53 of 53 tests in treeindex_commands.bats do exactly that). Reading the
# assertions cannot separate those; redirecting the binary can.
#
# Files with a non-zero DEFAULT failure count are reported as UNSTABLE and carry
# no classification: their baseline is not green, so the delta means nothing.

# PER-FILE TIMEOUT. Without this a single hanging file stalls the ENTIRE sweep,
# silently and forever: the run sits inside `d=$(bats "$f" ...)` producing no
# output, and the partial TSV looks exactly like a sweep that is merely slow.
# Measured 2026-08-14: the sweep stopped at row 93 of 98 on
# `tests/unit/test_diogenes.bats` and sat there for THREE AND A HALF HOURS.
#
# The file is not the problem -- it passes 19/19 in seconds when run standalone,
# under both the default binding AND `INTENT_BIN=/usr/bin/false`. The hang is
# environmental to this harness's context (backgrounded, no controlling tty),
# which is precisely the kind of difference a sweep must survive rather than
# diagnose.
#
# AND IT DID NOT REPRODUCE. A full sweep on 2026-08-15, backgrounded and with no
# tty, measured the same file cleanly as FULL and finished all 98 files in
# 7m52s. So the timeout was insurance on that run rather than the thing that
# saved it -- and the "sweep costs hours" belief this incident created was
# false: it cost minutes plus one hang. Keep the timeout (an intermittent hang
# is worse than a reproducible one, because it decides whether you trust the
# instrument), but do not let the folklore stand: re-running this is cheap, and
# treating it as expensive is what makes stale artefacts get deferred instead of
# fixed.
#
# A timed-out file is reported TIMEOUT and carries NO classification, for the
# same reason UNSTABLE does: a measurement that did not finish is not a
# measurement, and emitting a burn number for it would be inventing data. The
# sweep then continues, so ONE bad file costs one row instead of the whole run.
#
# GNU `timeout` is not on macOS by default; it arrives with coreutils, and CI
# runs a Linux leg. Detect once, and if neither spelling exists say so and run
# WITHOUT a timeout rather than silently skipping every file -- a sweep that
# quietly measured nothing is the failure this toolchain keeps refusing.
BURN_TIMEOUT="${BURN_TIMEOUT:-300}"
if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  TO=(timeout "$BURN_TIMEOUT")
elif command -v gtimeout >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  TO=(gtimeout "$BURN_TIMEOUT")
else
  echo "burn.sh: no timeout(1) or gtimeout(1) on PATH -- running WITHOUT a per-file timeout; a hanging file will stall the sweep" >&2
  TO=()
fi

set -uo pipefail
WT="${WT:?set WT}"
cd "$WT"

# OPT-IN TAP CAPTURE. With BURN_TAP_DIR set, both runs' raw TAP output is kept
# per file, so a downstream tool can name WHICH tests burn rather than only how
# many. This exists so per-test adjudication does not need its own copy of the
# run logic -- gen_pertest.sh reads these files and never invokes bats.
#
# One instrument, one measurement, two granularities of classification. The
# alternative was a second tool doing its own two runs per file, which is two
# copies of the thing that has to stay identical for the numbers to be
# comparable at all, and the exact drift lib_corpus.sh exists to catch.
#
# Both bindings are captured, not just the mutant one. The mutant `not ok` set
# IS the burning set ONLY IF the default run is green, so the consumer must be
# able to check that per file rather than trust the estate-level claim.
BURN_TAP_DIR="${BURN_TAP_DIR:-}"
if [ -n "$BURN_TAP_DIR" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$BURN_TAP_DIR" || { echo "burn.sh: cannot create BURN_TAP_DIR=$BURN_TAP_DIR" >&2; exit 2; }
fi
tap_slug() { printf '%s' "$1" | tr '/' '_'; }

printf 'FILE\tTESTS\tDEFAULT_FAIL\tBURN\tSTATUS\n'

for f in $(find tests -name '*.bats' | sort); do
  total=$(grep -c '^@test' "$f" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
  [ "$total" -gt 0 ] || continue
  # Capture the timeout's own exit code, not the pipeline's: `| grep` would
  # discard it and a timed-out run would report zero failures, which reads as a
  # clean pass. That is the same class as counting a file that never reached the
  # CLI as coverage.
  d_out="$("${TO[@]}" bats "$f" 2>&1)"; d_rc=$?
  m_out="$(INTENT_BIN=/usr/bin/false "${TO[@]}" bats "$f" 2>&1)"; m_rc=$?
  d=$(printf '%s' "$d_out" | grep -cE '^not ok' || true)
  m=$(printf '%s' "$m_out" | grep -cE '^not ok' || true)
  burn=$(( m - d ))
  [ "$burn" -lt 0 ] && burn=0

  # Keep the raw TAP for both bindings when asked. Written for EVERY file
  # including TIMEOUT and UNSTABLE ones, deliberately: the consumer needs to see
  # that a file's measurement was unusable, and a missing file would let it
  # infer "no failures" from an absence. Same reason a timed-out row is emitted
  # rather than dropped.
  if [ -n "$BURN_TAP_DIR" ]; then
    printf '%s\n' "$d_out" > "$BURN_TAP_DIR/$(tap_slug "$f").default.tap"
    printf '%s\n' "$m_out" > "$BURN_TAP_DIR/$(tap_slug "$f").mutant.tap"
  fi
  if [ "$d_rc" -eq 124 ] || [ "$m_rc" -eq 124 ]; then
    # 124 is timeout(1)'s "deadline reached". No classification: an unfinished
    # measurement is not a measurement.
    printf '%s\t%s\t--\t--\tTIMEOUT\n' "$f" "$total"
    continue
  elif [ "$d" -ne 0 ]; then
    status=UNSTABLE
  elif [ "$burn" -eq "$total" ]; then
    status=FULL
  elif [ "$burn" -eq 0 ]; then
    status=NONE
  else
    status=MIXED
  fi
  printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "$f" "$total" "$d" "$burn" "$status"
done

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# class_vocab_check.sh -- is every state that CLAIMS to be a parity class
# actually a class `parity.md` names? (AC-05.5, the vocabulary axis.)
#
# WHY THIS IS A SIBLING OF `corrected_check.sh` AND NOT A SECOND COPY OF IT.
# That check compares MEMBERSHIP within a class both documents already know
# about: which units `parity.md`'s `Corrected` section cites, against which
# units the table claims are `corrected`. **It is structurally blind to a class
# one document has and the other lacks** -- it can only compare the contents of
# a vocabulary, and nothing compared the vocabulary. vc named this on 2026-08-15
# as the same shape as the scope-from-prose defect in `corrected_check.sh`, one
# level up, and found it the way AC-05.5 predicts these are found: by accident,
# while verifying the mechanism built to stop finding them by accident.
#
# THE LIVE INSTANCE. `intent config` carries `target.state: undefined`, ratified
# "vc ruling, 2026-08-14 -- **the fifth parity class**, opened on this entry".
# The word `undefined` does not occur anywhere in `parity.md` -- whose own class
# list is introduced as "decided here, never discovered in triage". **The
# contract claiming sole authorship of the class list does not carry the fifth
# class**, and `corrected_check.sh` reports `agree exactly` while that is true.
#
# WHY `is_parity_class` IS DECLARED AND NOT DERIVED, which is AC-09.1's lesson
# applied one level up. The tempting rule is "a state that asserts a deviation
# must be grounded in parity.md" -- and it is wrong, measurably. `retire` asserts
# the largest deviation there is (the command does not ship) and belongs in NO
# class: all six retire rows carry their OWN ratification (hv rulings for
# organize / treeindex / st_zero, D09 for upgrade, AC-05.1 for help), so class
# membership is not their warrant and `parity.md` is not where it lives. The
# distinguishing fact is what a state CLAIMS about itself, which is judgement --
# so it is declared per state in `target_states`, where a human can be held to
# it, rather than inferred from a property that gets it wrong.
#
# It REPORTS and does not gate, matching its siblings, and refuses only on its
# own inability to measure.
# MUTATION PROOFS, run 2026-08-17 at `67814555` (ic). Co-located because a check
# whose failure path has never fired is a claim, not an instrument -- and this one
# is GATED into the pre-commit runner now, so it prints a verdict on every commit
# by four nodes. Re-run with the `TABLE=` / `PARITY=` overrides this file already
# reads; nothing else is needed.
#
#   control                          -> exit 0, "every claimed parity class is named"
#   a state claiming a class parity.md does not name
#                                    -> exit 0, reports `UNGROUNDED  zz-invented`
#   no state claims to be a parity class
#                                    -> exit 2 (line 52), never "all classes unused"
#   the class-block HEADING renamed  -> exit 2 (line 67), never "all claims ungrounded"
#   heading kept, bullet grammar broken
#                                    -> exit 2 (line 74)
#
# **The heading mutation is the one worth having.** Without that refusal a renamed
# heading empties `NAMED`, and every correctly-grounded class is then reported as
# ungrounded -- a wall of confident findings produced by reading nothing, pointing
# at the one file that is not wrong. The three empty-population guards were written
# before any of them had been fired; now they have been.
set -uo pipefail

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
PARITY_DIR="$(cd "$HERE/.." && pwd)"
ST_DIR="$(cd "$PARITY_DIR/.." && pwd)"
REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$ST_DIR/../../.." && pwd)"
TABLE="${TABLE:-$REPO_ROOT/surface/dispatch-table.json}"
PARITY="${PARITY:-$ST_DIR/parity.md}"

die() { echo "error: $1" >&2; exit 2; }

command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || die "jq is required and was not found on PATH"
[ -f "$TABLE" ]  || die "no dispatch table at $TABLE"
[ -f "$PARITY" ] || die "no parity contract at $PARITY"

# --- what the table declares a parity class ----------------------------------
CLAIMED="$(jq -r '(.target_states // [])[] | select(.is_parity_class == true) | .state' "$TABLE" | sort -u)"
[ -n "$CLAIMED" ] || die "\`target_states\` declares no state a parity class -- with a populated vocabulary that is a schema change or a bad query, and reporting every parity.md class as unused would be the wrong answer to it"

# --- what parity.md NAMES as a class -----------------------------------------
# Scoped to the sub-bullets under the ratified-deviation-class heading, NOT to
# the whole file, and that is deliberate: `retire` occurs in `parity.md` inside
# the register's column grammar (`keep · retire · deviate`), so a whole-file
# match would report it grounded as a CLASS on the strength of a table header.
# **Deciding scope by where a word happens to appear is the defect this
# directory has already shipped once** -- corrected_check.sh matched the literal
# string `parity.md` in a ratification and put three cited units out of scope.
CLASS_BLOCK="$(awk '
  /^- \*\*Ratified deviation classes/ { inblock = 1; next }
  inblock && /^- / { inblock = 0 }
  inblock { print }
' "$PARITY")"
[ -n "$CLASS_BLOCK" ] || die "found no ratified-deviation-class block in $PARITY -- the heading \`- **Ratified deviation classes\` did not match, so the class list could not be read. Refusing rather than reporting every claimed class as ungrounded, which is what an empty class list would produce."

NAMED="$(printf '%s\n' "$CLASS_BLOCK" \
  | sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*-[[:space:]]*\*\*\([^*]*\)\*\*.*/\1/p' \
  | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' \
  | sed 's/[[:space:]]*$//' \
  | grep -v '^$' | sort -u)"
[ -n "$NAMED" ] || die "the ratified-deviation-class block in $PARITY names no classes -- the bullet grammar (\`  - **Name** -- ...\`) did not match anything inside it"

# --- the comparison -----------------------------------------------------------
UNGROUNDED="$(comm -23 <(printf '%s\n' "$CLAIMED") <(printf '%s\n' "$NAMED"))"
GROUNDED="$(comm -12 <(printf '%s\n' "$CLAIMED") <(printf '%s\n' "$NAMED"))"

printf 'class-vocab: the table declares %d state(s) a parity class; parity.md names %d class(es); %d grounded\n' \
  "$(printf '%s\n' "$CLAIMED"  | grep -c .)" \
  "$(printf '%s\n' "$NAMED"    | grep -c .)" \
  "$(printf '%s\n' "$GROUNDED" | grep -c .)"

if [ -n "$UNGROUNDED" ]; then
  printf '\nclass-vocab: states CLAIM to be a parity class and parity.md does not name one:\n'
  printf '%s\n' "$UNGROUNDED" | sed 's/^/  UNGROUNDED  /'
